Read a tree-volume regression model

Source: vignettes/regression-output.Rmd
regression-output.Rmd

How much does a tree’s estimated timber volume change with trunk diameter, after accounting for height? We will read one regression result and connect its coefficients, uncertainty and residual error. In this sample, an extra inch of diameter is associated with about 4.71 extra cubic feet of volume at a fixed height. The remaining residual scatter is about 3.88 cubic feet.

Understand the measurements

Example data: R’s built-in trees dataset

The 31 observations are felled black cherry trees. Volume is timber volume in cubic feet and Height is height in feet. Despite its name, Girth is trunk diameter, measured in inches at 4 feet 6 inches above the ground. Reading the data documentation matters: interpreting this column as circumference would give the slope the wrong physical meaning.

library(olsrr)
tree_data <- datasets::trees
stopifnot(nrow(tree_data) == 31L, !anyNA(tree_data))
head(tree_data)
#>   Girth Height Volume
#> 1   8.3     70   10.3
#> 2   8.6     65   10.3
#> 3   8.8     63   10.2
#> 4  10.5     72   16.4
#> 5  10.7     81   18.8
#> 6  10.8     83   19.7

Every row has all three measurements, so no tree is dropped. This example describes associations in the observed trees. It does not establish a growth law or show what an intervention on height would cause. Keeping the units beside the data helps distinguish a coefficient from a measure without units, such as R-squared.

Fit one model 

volume_model <- lm(Volume ~ Girth + Height, data = tree_data)

This additive model lets volume change linearly with diameter and height. Each slope describes a comparison holding the other predictor fixed. The formula does not encode the geometric relationship between diameter and volume, which might motivate a curved or transformed model later. For now the aim is to understand exactly what this fitted summary says.

Read the regression table 

ols_regress(volume_model)
#>                          Model Summary                          
#> ---------------------------------------------------------------
#> R                       0.974       RMSE                 3.882 
#> R-Squared               0.948       MSE                 15.069 
#> Adj. R-Squared          0.944       Coef. Var           12.866 
#> Pred R-Squared          0.931       AIC                176.910 
#> MAE                     2.956       SBC                182.646 
#> ---------------------------------------------------------------
#>  RMSE: Root Mean Square Error 
#>  MSE: Mean Square Error 
#>  MAE: Mean Absolute Error 
#>  AIC: Akaike Information Criteria 
#>  SBC: Schwarz Bayesian Criteria 
#> 
#>                                  ANOVA                                  
#> -----------------------------------------------------------------------
#>                 Sum of                                                 
#>                Squares        DF    Mean Square       F           Sig. 
#> -----------------------------------------------------------------------
#> Regression    7684.163         2       3842.081    254.972    < 0.0001 
#> Residual       421.921        28         15.069                        
#> Total         8106.084        30                                       
#> -----------------------------------------------------------------------
#> 
#>                                      Parameter Estimates                                       
#> ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
#>       model       Beta    Std. Error    Std. Beta      t         Sig         lower      upper 
#> ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
#> (Intercept)    -57.988         8.638                 -6.713    < 0.0001    -75.682    -40.293 
#>       Girth      4.708         0.264        0.899    17.816    < 0.0001      4.167      5.249 
#>      Height      0.339         0.130        0.132     2.607      0.0145      0.073      0.606 
#> ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The Beta estimate for Girth, 4.708, means about 4.71 additional cubic feet per additional inch of diameter, comparing trees of the same height. For Height, 0.339 means about 0.34 additional cubic feet per extra foot of height at a fixed diameter. Standardized betas express effects on a different scale; use the unstandardized Beta column for these statements in inches, feet and cubic feet.

The Std. Error column measures uncertainty in each estimated slope. The lower and upper columns give its 95% confidence interval under the model assumptions: about 4.17 to 5.25 for diameter and 0.073 to 0.606 for height. The height estimate is less precise relative to its size. These intervals concern conditional mean slopes, not the volumes of individual trees. The p-values test zero coefficients conditional on the other term; they do not measure the probability that a predictor matters.

The intercept is about -57.99 cubic feet at zero diameter and zero height. Neither value describes a tree in this sample. This is a warning against extrapolation, rather than evidence of negative timber volume.

Connect the output to base R 

base_summary <- summary(volume_model)
knitr::kable(base_summary$coefficients[, c("Estimate", "Std. Error")],
             digits = 3, caption = "The same coefficients and standard errors from summary(lm(...)).")
The same coefficients and standard errors from summary(lm(…)).
Estimate Std. Error
(Intercept) -57.988 8.638
Girth 4.708 0.264
Height 0.339 0.130

The estimates and standard errors agree with the parameter table above: olsrr presents information from the same fitted model. R’s residual standard error, base_summary$sigma, is the RMSE reported here. Its value of 3.882 cubic feet is the square root of residual sum of squares divided by 28 residual degrees of freedom. It describes remaining scatter, not a fixed error allowance for each new prediction.

Understand the ANOVA decomposition

The regression output already includes an ANOVA table. ols_anova() lets you request just that part when the overall fit is your question.

volume_anova <- ols_anova(volume_model)
volume_anova

In that table, the total sum of squares, 8106.084, divides into 7684.163 attributed to the regression and 421.921 left in the residuals. Dividing 7684.163 by 8106.084 gives R-squared, 0.948. This is variation explained in these trees, not a percentage accuracy guarantee for future volumes.

There are two regression degrees of freedom, one for each slope, and 28 residual degrees of freedom: 31 observations minus three estimated coefficients, including the intercept. Dividing each sum of squares by its degrees of freedom gives the mean squares. Their ratio is the overall F statistic, 254.972. Its null is that both slopes are zero. This joint test does not identify which model shape is adequate or validate the error assumptions.

The concrete next task is to inspect residual shape and spread before relying on the confidence intervals. Continue with residual diagnostics, or revisit getting started. The help for ols_regress() and ols_anova() covers the remaining table fields and supported interfaces.
